title-group.article-title: Nutshell Combustion Soot as a Sustainable Carbon Material: From Morphology to Electrochemical and Adsorptive Performance

abstract.p: Converting waste materials to value-added products is a key strategy for sustainable resource management. In this study, soot generated from the combustion of various biomass sourcesincluding apricot (AP) shells, pistachio (PS) shells, hazelnut (HZ) shells, a combination of apricot and pistachio shells, and a mixture of hazelnut, apricot, and pistachio shellswas collected and systematically characterized using SEM–EDS, BET, XRD, Raman spectroscopy, and FTIR analysis. The result obtained shows that the HZ + AP + PS soot has the largest surface area (76.66 m2/g), highest mass % of carbon (75.65%), abundant oxygen-containing functional groups, and some heteroatoms, which contribute to its promising potential in various applications such as sensors, supercapacitors, batteries, and water treatment. The electrochemical performance of the carbon soot samples using cyclic voltammetry (CV) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) demonstrated promising redox activity, particularly in the HZ + AP + PS soot materials, which exhibited the highest electrochemical performance due to a high specific surface area, while the HZ soot exhibited the lowest, suggesting a promising electrode material for the electrochemical reaction. Additionally, batch adsorption experiments demonstrated that all soot samples efficiently removed Pb­(II) and norfloxacin antibiotic from aqueous solutions, achieving adsorption efficiencies of ∼91% at pH 6 and up to ∼99% within 60 min. The HZ + AP + PS soot shows a high electrochemical performance in the detection of streptomycin. The novel findings in this work indicate that the ternary biomass-derived carbon (HZ + AP + PS) soot has substantial potential as a sustainable and cost-effective material for electrochemical applications (sensors, batteries, or supercapacitors) and as an efficient adsorbent for water detoxification.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The transformation of material traditionally viewed as waste into valuable resources, fostering sustainability and economic opportunity, is a concept that perfectly aligns with a sustainable management approach. Studies estimate that close to 50% of the global population uses solid biomass as their main source of energy for domestic purposes. In the Asian continent, the commonly used fuel in rural areas is solid biomass, which results in the excessive production of black carbon, making it the second most important source known as household biomass combustion among other sources such as vehicles, industries, fossil fuel burning, and forest fires. ,

Carbon soot, a fine, black, amorphous carbon-based material formed as a byproduct of the combustion of biomass such as wood, agricultural residues, or other organic matter with impurities, is regarded as a pollutant. Unlike carbon soot, activated carbon is manufactured industrially and exhibits a higher C/O ratio. Due to their distinctive physicochemical characteristics, including high surface area, porosity, and surface functional groups, these small-sized pollutant soot particles have the capacity to adsorb a variety of pollutants, including organic pollutants such as volatile organic compounds, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and heavy metal ions. The negative impact of these carbon soots ranges from their environmental impact, such as contribution to global warming and as carcinogenic material, as classified by the World Health Organization (WHO), to allergic respiratory disease affecting human health. These environmental and health concerns may potentially be eased through sustainable conversion/isolation of soot from pollution into functional materials with a positive impact in various industries. For instance, carbon-rich soot can be processed into nanomaterials applications with electronics and catalysis, fertilizer additives, pigments and reinforcement in automobile tires, a conductive material in lithium-ion battery manufacture, adsorbents for air and water treatment to eliminate different pollutants, and energy storage system such as supercapacitors. Therefore, to tackle environmental challenges and foster sustainable wealth creation, it is crucial to recognize carbon soot (an inexpensive and abundant material) as a valuable resource through innovative applications.

Recently, there has been a growing trend in nations with harsh winter conditions to utilize biomass waste from fruits, especially nutshells, as a substitute for traditional fuels such as wood, coal, or gas. Nutshells are renewable, biodegradable, and carbon-neutral biomass sources, making them an environmentally friendly option. Additionally, many nutshells possess a high calorific value, allowing them to serve as an efficient and sustainable fuel. Since they are often agricultural byproducts, their use reduces waste while providing an abundant and cost-effective energy source, particularly in regions with a thriving nut processing industry.

Nevertheless, the combustion of nutshells in heaters results in the generation of soot, which tends to accumulate in the upper parts of the heaters. During combustion, hot gases carrying soot particles rise due to thermal convection. As the temperature decreases in the upper regions, soot tends to condense and accumulate more efficiently, leading to a higher deposition rate compared to those in lower parts. In most cases, this soot is simply discarded or washed away without being repurposed. Due to its carbon-rich nature, this byproduct holds untapped potential for a range of value-added applications, including its utilization in energy storage materials, as adsorbents for environmental remediation, and as electroactive materials in sensor technologies. In recent efforts, researchers have applied biomass-derived soot as an adsorbent to remove heavy metals from aqueous solutions. From the previous literature, small, branched carbon nanotubes, carbon nano-onions, and graphitic nanosheets were extracted from kerosene, diesel, and petrol soot with promising potential application in electrode material preparation, energy storage and harvesting, metal-ion sensing, photodegradation, and adsorption of organic pollutants from water. , Fatima and Iram collected plastic fuel-derived soot as an adsorbent of Ni, Pb, and Cr from their aqueous solutions. The maximum efficiency for Pb, Ni, and Cr was 82.1%, 64%, and 82.5% at the contact time of 120 min and optimum pH 9. Zhou et al. prepared surface-modified nanoscale carbon black to remove Cu­(II) and Cd­(II) from an aqueous solution, and the maximum adsorption quantities obtained were 27.8 and 31.7 mg·g–1, respectively. Diesel particulate filter (DPF) soot demonstrated high adsorption capacities of 51.1 mg g–1 for Cd­(II) and 25.0 mg g–1 for Cu­(II) at pH 4 compared to commercial activated carbon. However, due to its tunable porous structure, large surface area, excellent electrical conductivity, and good chemical/thermal stability, it can serve as an electrode material for various electrode designs and applications. For supercapacitor application, silk-derived hierarchical porous carbon demonstrated a high specific capacitance of 242 F g–1, a high-energy density of 102 W h kg–1 (48 W h L–1), as well as an excellent cycling life stability (9% loss after 10,000 cycles). Yang et al. produced hierarchical porous biochar derived from jujube fruits, which exhibits an electrochemical capacitance of 587 F g–1 in an aqueous electrolyte. Hristea et al. produced a hybrid spruce-bark-graphene oxide compound (HySB) as an electrode material for supercapacitors, where a higher capacitive performance of 530.5 μF cm–2 was obtained compared to the commercial (reference) electrode material (SLC1512P graphite) with 150.3 μF cm–2 capacitance. Excellent electrochemical stability, good frequency-response ability, and AC filtering performances in both aqueous and organic electrolytes were obtained when the soot-graphene hybrid structure was developed as an supercapacitor electrode. Electrochemical properties of waste frying oil-derived carbon nano-onions in a device were investigated, and the results show a wide potential range of 1.9 V and specific capacitance (C S) of 342 F g–1 (at a current density of 0.5 A g–1) with an energy density (E d) of 164.33 W h kg–1 by retaining 83% of its original capacity after 10,000 charge–discharge cycles. A castor oil-derived soot@MoS2 hybrid bifunctional electrode device was produced, where the electrode investigated shows a high specific capacitance (C S) of 129.89 F g–1 and an energy density (E d)/maximum power density (P d) of 25.69 W h kg–1/1666.6 W kg–1 with a cyclic stability of 81.4% for 5000 cycles.

In this work, we explored the potential of the carbon soot derived from biomass sources, such as apricot (AP) shells, pistachio (PS) shells, hazelnut (HZ) shells, AP + PS (1:1) shells, and HZ + AP + PS (1:1:1) shells, obtained from the upper parts of the heaters. The structural and morphological features of the various samples are analyzed by Raman spectroscopy, Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy, energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and X-ray diffraction (XRD), followed by electrochemical performance using cyclic voltammetry and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. A practical application focusing on conductivity, the removal of Pb­(II) and norfloxacin antibiotic from an aqueous solution, and electrochemical performance on streptomycin was implemented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the carbon soot samples in real-world scenarios.

sec.title: Chemical and Reagents
sec.p: Nitric acid, hydrochloric acid, lead nitrate, potassium bromide, acetonitrile, norfloxacin, streptomycin, and potassium ferricyanide were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich Co., Ltd. Milli-Q water was used throughout the experiment. Dimethylformamide (DMF) (99.8%) was obtained from Sigma-Aldrich (Darmstadt, Germany). All chemicals and reagents used in the experiments were of analytical grade and were used without further purification.

sec.title: Apparatus
sec.p: A GPR-11H30D DC power supply (Gw Instek, China) was employed, which has an adjustable voltage range of 0–110 V and a current range of 0–3 A. An ultrasonic bath cleanser (CREST model 575D, Singapore) was utilized to sonicate the obtained HZ + AP + PS soot.

sec.title: Soot Samples
sec.p: Biomass-derived soot samples collected from the upper parts of heaters (cover and chimney holes) were utilized in this study. Waste apricot shell (AP), pistachio shell (PS), hazelnut shell (HZ), AP + PS, and HZ + AP + PS served as fuel sources, and the resulting fine soot powder samples underwent various analytical techniques. Soot in the upper regions is often loosely deposited and easier to scrape off compared to areas closer to the flame, where it might be more compact or mixed with residues. The lower parts of heaters may have more impurities from incomplete combustion, ash, or external contaminants, whereas the upper parts provide a relatively cleaner soot. Collecting from the upper parts ensures uniformity in sampling locations, leading to better reproducibility and comparability in experimental studies.

sec.title: Characterization of the Carbon Soot Material
Surface Characteristics
sec.p: All the soot samples were characterized directly without any pretreatment step. The surface morphologies, elemental mapping, and elemental composition of the soot samples were analyzed by using a scanning electron microscope equipped with an energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometer (SEM–EDS, JEOL IT-300). Raman spectra were obtained from an INVIA Raman microscope with a 514 nm Ar laser (Renishaw, UK). The Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectrum was measured on a Thermo Fisher Scientific Nicolet iS50 FT-IR spectrometer in the region of 4000–400 cm–1 using KBr pellets. The crystalline phases of the composite were characterized using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Rigaku) equipped with a Cu laser source generated at 35 mA and 40 kV at a scanning rate of 5°/min between the diffraction angle (2θ) of 5° to 90°. Characteristics of the specific surface area, total pore volume, and BHJ pore diameter were estimated using a N2 adsorption–desorption (BELSORP-mini) BET analyzer at 77 K. An inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, ICAP DUO 6500) was used to determine Pb­(II). High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC, FLEXAR, PerkinElmer, China) was used to determine the norfloxacin antibiotic.

sec.title: Electrochemical Measurement
sec.p: The electrochemical characterization (cyclic voltammetry and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy) experiments were carried out using an EmStat4s potentiostat (PalmSens, The Netherlands), operated by PSTrace 5.9 software. A triple electrode system of a screen-printed carbon electrode (SPE) (Quasense, Thailand) containing a carbon counter electrode, a carbon working electrode, and a silver/silver chloride reference electrode was used for all measurements.

The carbon soot dispersions were formulated in an ethanolic/water medium at a concentration of 1 mg/mL and subsequently subjected to ultrasonic treatment for 60 min. The CS/SPEs were prepared through drop casting, utilizing 6 μL of CS dispersions on bare carbon SPE, followed by the evaporation of the solvent at 37 °C. Electrochemical measurements were conducted in drop (70 μL) detection mode using the cyclic voltammetry at a potential window from −0.3 V to +0.6 V at a scan rate of 50 mV/s.

sec.title: Detection of Streptomycin
sec.p: The soot with the highest electrochemical performance from the cyclic voltammetry (HZ + AP + PS) was selected for detection of streptomycin using differential pulse voltammetry (DPV). The carbon soot dispersions were formulated in an ethanolic/water (3:2 and 2:2) and water only at a concentration of 3 and 5 mg/mL and subsequently subjected to ultrasonic treatment for 60 min. The CS/SPEs were prepared through drop casting, utilizing 6 μL of CS dispersions on bare carbon SPE, followed by the evaporation of the solvent at 37 °C. The concentration of streptomycin to be detected was 1000 ppm in Milli-Q water. Electrochemical measurements were conducted in drop (70 μL) detection mode using differential pulse voltammetry (DPV) at a potential window from 0.0 to 1.3 V at a scan rate of 50 mV/s.

sec.title: Batch Adsorption
sec.p: The batch mode adsorption studies were conducted in 60 mL polyethylene bottles by agitating 0.015 g of carbon soot of the apricot shell (AP), pistachio shell (PS), h shell (HZ), AP + PS shell, and HZ + AP + PS shell in 10 mL of 10 mg/L Pb­(II) and norfloxacin antibiotic solution on a shaker at 30 rpm at room temperature for 60 min. Then, the solution was filtered using 0.20 μm, and the residual concentration of Pb­(II) and norfloxacin antibiotic aqueous solution was measured via an inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES) and HPLC-UV.

The adsorption amount q e (mg/g) at equilibrium and the removal efficiency (% R) of the adsorbent were calculated using the following equations: 1 qe=[(C0−Ce)×V]/m
2 %R=[(C0−Ce)/C0]×100 where C 0 and C e are the initial and equilibrium concentrations (mg/L), respectively; m is the mass of the adsorbent (g); and V is the volume of the solution (L).

sec.title: SEM–EDS Analysis
sec.p: The morphologies of the apricot shell soot (AP), pistachio shell soot (PS), hazelnut shell soot (HZ), AP + PS soot, and HZ + AP + PS soot samples were investigated using SEM, as shown in Figure . All observed soot particle samples exhibited significant surface roughness and agglomerated to form relatively complex structures, indicating that increased surface roughness provides a larger external surface area, thereby suggesting a greater availability of adsorption sites on the soot surface. The elemental analysis data (Figure , Table ) showed that the apricot shell (AP) soot, hazelnut shell (HZ) soot, pistachio shell (PS) soot, pistachio + apricot shell (AP + PS) soot, and HZ + AP + PS soot have different compositions. In the apricot shell (AP) soot (Figure a), elements such as C, O, S, K, and Na were observed, with significantly high S and K. In the pistachio shell (PS) soot (Figure b), elements such as C, O, N, S, Cl, K, and Na were observed. In the AP + PS (1:1) soot (Figure c), elements such as C, O, S, K, and Na were observed with less mass % of S and K without the presence of Cl and N. In the hazelnut shell (HZ) soot (Figure d), elements such as C and O were observed with less significance of S, Cl, K, P, Ca, and Na. The HZ + AP + PS soot (Figure e), which consists of a mixture of AP, PS, and HZ (1:1:1), shows elements such as C and O with less significant S, K, and Na. From our observations, the HZ + AP + PS soot has the highest mass % of carbon (75.65%), suggesting a material with a smaller particle size and large surface area that is rough, disordered, and amorphous (confirmed from Raman (Figure )) with a network of pores as shown in Figure e­(i,ii), which can also be confirmed from the BET results of the HZ + AP + PS soot (Table ). Hence, this vital surface property influences its application for adsorption, catalysis, or electrochemistry.

sec.title: FTIR Analysis
sec.p: Functional group analysis of the various soot samples obtained using FTIR spectroscopy is shown in Figure . The major components of biomass are cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. The broad peaks at the wavenumbers 3418, 3444, 3456, and 3447 cm–1 are for PS, HZ, AP + PS, and HZ + AP + PS, respectively, and the less intense peak of AP at 3431 cm–1, which indicated the stretching vibration of OH groups due to the existence of a hydrogen bond and reduction of water and cellulose contents. The intense peak at the wavelength of 1641, 1519, 1511, 1592, 1592, and 1587 cm–1, respectively, for AP, PS, HZ, AP + PS, and HZ + AP + PS corresponds to the carboxylic acid (−COOH) group to represent the existence of carbonyl groups (–CO) and carboxylic acid resulting from the hemicellulose structure, respectively. The intensity peak between 1392 and 1446 cm–1, 1353 and 1475, 1349 and 1475, 1351 and 1478, and 1346 and 1481 cm–1 for AP, PS, HZ, AP + PS, and HZ + AP + PS, respectively, may be assigned to aromatic skeleton vibrations combined with C–H in-plane deformations. , The band peak at 1132, 1163, 1291, and 1109 cm–1 of the AP, PS, HZ, and AP + PS soot, respectively, confirmed the presence of C–O–C and C–OH functional group stretching due to the presence of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. , The peaks at 696 cm–1 for AP, 703 cm–1 for HZ, 634 cm–1 for AP + PS, and 696 cm–1 for HZ + AP + PS confirm the presence of aromatic and heteroaromatic compounds by C–H wagging vibrations of all soot samples except in the PS soot. Hence, the presence of various oxygen-containing groups (hydroxyl, carboxyl, and epoxide groups) among the soot structure, which is a potential active site that can interact with positively charged heavy metals such as Pb­(II), Cd­(II), or Zn­(II) via electrostatic interaction or complexation, suggests its capability for various applications such as adsorbents, electrode materials, and catalysis.

sec.title: N2 Adsorption–Desorption Isotherm
sec.p: In Figure , the BET surface area and pore-size distribution of the AP, PS, HZ, AP + PS, and HZ + AP + PS soot were determined. The N2 adsorption/desorption isotherm curve of the AP, PS, HZ, AP + PS, and HZ + AP + PS soot exhibited a Type-IV shape, which is a typical characteristic of mesoporous materials, according to the IUPAC classification as shown in Figure , which is effective for the adsorption of inorganic and organic contaminants from aqueous solutions. From Table , the HZ + AP + PS soot has the highest surface area, pore volume, and small particle size, indicating that it has more active sites available for the adsorption of target analytes compared with other soot materials. From Barrett–Joyner–Halenda data (BJH), the mean pore diameter of all the soot materials was 2–50 nm, indicating that materials have mesoporous structures and are essential for various applications such as water decontamination and sensor development.

sec.title: XRD Analysis
sec.p: The XRD profile of the soot samples, which provides insights into their mineral phases, is presented in Figure . Numerous mineral phases were present, as evidenced by the study of the XRD patterns. The soot samples exhibited narrow and distinct bands over the analyzed 2θ, which can be attributed to the presence of inorganic components within the carbon chain. In AP, the peaks at 23.76°, 25.37°, 26.26°, 28.32°, 29.95°, and 30.84° represent the characteristic peaks of graphite, showing that the soot material contains crystalline graphite that is highly ordered with a layered crystalline structure, which is the most recognizable crystallographic structure. The peaks at 35.71°, 37.04°, 37.78°, 40.58°, and 43.38° represent turbostratic (having both sp2 and sp3 characters) graphite, which reveals a disordered arrangement of graphite layers in the carbon structure. The peaks from 17.70° to 35.58° were assigned to cellulose and hemicellulose, respectively. In PS crystalline patterns, the intense peaks at 24.28°, 26.70°, 28.34°, 29.51°, 30.44°, and 31.38° represent the characteristic peaks of graphite, showing that the soot material contains crystalline graphite that is highly ordered with a layered crystalline structure, which is the most recognizable crystallographic structure. The peaks at 33.05°, 35.58°, 40.58°, and 44.32° represent turbostratic graphite, which reveals a disordered arrangement of graphite layers in the carbon structure. The intense peaks from 21.83° to 35.58° were assigned to cellulose and hemicellulose, respectively. In HZ, the less intense peaks at 25.38°, 26.56°, 28.32°, 29.37°, 30.84°, and 31.43° represent the characteristic peaks of graphite, showing that the soot material contains crystalline graphite that is less ordered with a layered crystalline structure, which is the most recognizable crystallographic structure. The peaks at 35.58°, 40.58°, and 43.24° represent turbostratic graphite, which reveals a more disordered arrangement of graphite layers in the carbon structure. The intense peaks from 21.76° to 35.58° were assigned to cellulose and hemicellulose, respectively. In AP + PS, the peaks at 24.41°, 25.52°, 26.56°, 28.47°, 29.73°, 30.98°, and 31.57° represent the characteristic peaks of graphite, showing that the soot material contains crystalline graphite that is ordered with a layered crystalline structure, which is the most recognizable crystallographic structure. The peaks at 35.85°, 37.18°, 38.66°, 40.53°, 43.56°, 44.73°, and 43.24° represent turbostratic graphite, which reveals a more disordered arrangement of graphite layers in the carbon structure. The intense peaks from 18.13° to 40.53° were assigned to cellulose and hemicellulose, respectively. In HZ + AP + PS, the peaks at 24.19°, 25.52°, 26.56°, 28.18°, 29.65°, 30.32°, and 31.43° represent the characteristic peaks of graphite, showing that the soot material contains crystalline graphite that is ordered with a layered crystalline structure, which is the most recognizable crystallographic structure. The peaks at 35.71°, 40.58°, 43.38°, and 44.73° represent turbostratic graphite, which reveals a disordered arrangement of graphene layers in the carbon structure. The intense peaks from 15.47° to 35.71° were assigned to cellulose and hemicellulose, respectively. However, the graphitization of carbon is visible, and the degree of disorder is determined from the degree of peak shortening and the relative strength of the dispersed peaks. However, it was observed that intense peaks at 28.32° and 29.51° in the AP and PS soot are more visible, indicating ordered and graphitic structure compared to the peaks in the HZ, AP + PS, and HZ + AP + PS soot.

sec.title: Raman Spectra
sec.p: The Raman spectra of AP, PS, HZ, AP + PS, and HZ + AP + PS are shown in Figure . As typical for disordered graphene, three significant Raman bands, which correspond to the D band at 1373 cm–1, the G band at 1594 cm–1, and the 2D peak at roughly 2329 cm–1, were clearly visible. The G-band is associated with the E2g phonon of sp2-hybridized carbon atoms linked to graphitic carbon. In contrast, the D band corresponds to the K-point phonons of sp3-hybridized carbon atoms, which are indicative of structural defects or partially disordered arrangements in graphitic materials. The 2D band also provides useful information about the stacking order. The broadness of these peaks indicates the amorphous nature of soot, and the G peak was found to be more intense in the PS soot as compared to that of other soot. The intensity ratio of the D band to G band (I D/I G) obtained was 0.91, 0.88, 0.98, 0.98, and 0.99 for the AP, PS, HZ, AP + PS, and HZ + AP + PS soot, respectively, which is due to a vast significant number of the sp2-hybridized carbon domains that lead to the introduction of the more structural disorder. The AP and PS soot exhibited a lower intensity ratio, suggesting a more ordered and graphitic structure with a lower degree of carbon disorder compared to those of the HZ, AP + PS, and HZ + AP + PS soot. The latter samples displayed nearly identical intensity ratios and 2D band characteristics, as further evidenced by the XRD pattern (Figure ). Hence, the HZ + AP + PS soot with the highest intensity ratio reflects a higher degree of disorder, which corresponds to a higher surface area (similar to BET results in Table ) due to more defects, which in turn enhances the charge transport property and adsorption efficiency of the carbon soot sample, , indicating that the surface properties of the HZ + AP + PS soot are very vital for electrochemical reaction and adsorption. Based on graphitization, the AP, PS, HZ, AP + PS, and HZ + AP + PS soot have a larger surface area compared with other soot-based materials such as cotton soot (I D/I G = 1.03) based on the intensity ratio in the Raman spectra.

sec.title: Cyclic Voltammetry
sec.p: The electrochemical characteristics of the AP, PS, HZ, AP + PS, and HZ + AP + PS soot in K3Fe­(CN)6 were investigated by cyclic voltammetry using a screen-printed carbon electrode (SPCE) under a potential window from −0.3 to +0.6 V at a scan rate of 50 mVs–1, and the results are reported in Figure a. The bare screen-printed carbon electrode (SPCE) exhibited two distinct redox peaks. After modification of the SPCE surface with AP, PS, HZ, AP + PS, and HZ + AP + PS, the redox peak current value significantly increased as expected, in which the HZ + AP + PS/SPCE gives the highest peak current value, which is slightly higher than that of AP + PS, PS, and AP/SPCE compared to HZ/SPCE with the least peak current value.

caption.p: (a) Cyclic voltammogram and (b) Nyquist plot of bare/SPCE, AP/SPCE, PS/SPCE, HZ/SPCE, AP + PS/SPCE, and HZ + AP + PS (HAP)/SPCE. Supporting electrolyte: 5 mM K3Fe­(CN)6. Frequency range: 0.1 Hz to 100 kHz. Scan rate: 50 mV s–1.

sec.p: The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) analysis was performed to compare the interface resistances of the different modified electrodes and to better comprehend the improved electrochemical performance. The Nyquist plots (Figure b) show two distinct parts: the electron transfer process is represented by a semicircle in the high-frequency region, while electron diffusion is represented by a linear component in the low-frequency zone. Hence, the diameter of the semicircles observed will be used to determine the values of the charge-transfer resistance (R ct) of modified electrodes. , The Nyquist plot (Figure b) compares the resistances of the AP, PS, HZ, AP + PS, and HZ + AP + PS soot samples. The result shows that the resistance of the AP + PS and HZ + AP + PS soot is much smaller than that of AP and PS, with HZ having the highest resistance, demonstrating better electron transfer at the surface of the HZ + AP + PS/SPCE electrode. According to Qiu et al., electrochemical performance of a biomass-derived carbon material depends on its large specific surface area, suitable pore structure, surface modification, and superior electrical conductivity. This is because carbon materials containing a mesoporous structure (2–50 nm in diameter) and layered pore structure can provide a channel for the rapid transfer of electrolyte ions and accelerates the transfer rate of electrolyte ions, thereby increasing the bilayer capacitance. The surface functional groups and heteroatoms on biomass-derived carbon also can provide more pseudocapacitance through reversible redox reactions, which can be used as a complement to the bilayer capacitance to improve the electrochemical performance of carbon electrode materials. However, the highest electrochemical performance exhibited by the HZ + AP + PS soot is due to its large specific surface area and mesoporous structure compared to the AP, PS, and HZ soot (as shown in Table ), leading to a more exposed electroactive site and faster diffusion, which improved their electrochemical response, thereby suggesting their promising conductivity properties. , The presence of heteroatoms such as sulfur, nitrogen, phosphorus, or calcium in the soot structure, as confirmed by the EDS results (Table ) provides a key function in the electrode material as electron donors, influencing the surface’s hydrophilicity, electron conductivity, and cycling stability, which also contribute significantly to the high electrochemical performance of other soot materials. The low electrochemical performance and high transfer resistance of AP, PS, and HZ soot materials can be attributed to the low surface area and pore volume, resulting in diminished conductivity, as shown in Table . However, the CV responses are consistent with the EIS changes, which further confirmed the electrochemical potential of the carbon soot material is in the order as follows: HZ + AP + PS > AP + PS > PS > AP > HZ. As a result, HZ + AP + PS (HAP), AP + PS, PS, and AP appear to be promising materials for electrochemistry.

sec.title: Detection of Streptomycin
sec.p: As shown in Figure a and b, HZ + AP + PS (HAP) was selected for the detection of streptomycin based on its high electrochemical performance. Two types of concentration (3 and 5 mg mL–1) with an ethanol/water ratio (3:2 and 2:2) and concentration (3 and 5 mg mL–1) with water only were investigated using the drop-cast method. The results in Figure show streptomycin peak currents measured by the DPV technique using the modified SPEs of two different concentrations and formulation ratios. The optimized parameter for detecting streptomycin using the DPV technique was obtained from a previous literature work. As observed in Figure , compared to the unmodified SPE (bare), the modified SPE at different concentrations and formulation ratios shows a high current, in which the modified SPE with 3 mg mL–1 (water only) shows a very high peak current. The signal was 7 times higher than that of the bare SPE, and the streptomycin peak potential shifted from 0.893 V on bare SPE to 0.799 V on 3 mg mL–1 (water only) HZ + AP + PS (HAP)-modified SPEs. Hence, 3 mg mL–1 (water only) HZ + AP + PS (HAP)-modified SPE will be selected as a highly effective modifying material for streptomycin detection in further studies.

caption.p: Differential pulse voltammograms of 1000 mg L–1 of (a) bare/SPCE and (b) 3 mg/mL (water only) HZ + AP + PS/SPCE. Supporting electrolyte: 0.1 M BRB; pH 9; scan rate: 100 mV/s.

sec.title: HZ + AP + PS Soot Ink-Coated Paper for an Electrically Conductive Substrate
sec.p: A concentration (5 mg mL–1) of the HZ + AP + PS soot was added to DMF to form a long-lasting suspension solution. The HZ + AP + PS suspension was applied directly onto filter paper and subsequently dried to create a conductive sheet. Consequently, the HZ + AP + PS filter paper exhibited a low resistance of 3.33 Ω sq–1, making it suitable for use as a conductor to power LEDs (Figure ).

sec.title: Adsorption Experiment
sec.p: As shown in Table , AP, PS, HZ, AP + PS, and HZ + AP + PS soot materials were utilized as adsorbents in the removal of Pb­(II) and the norfloxacin antibiotic. The adsorption efficiency of Pb­(II) was found to be 91.71 ± 0.14%, 91.11 ± 0.22%, 91.59 ± 0.16%, 91.65 ± 0.19%, and 91.76 ± 0.18%, while the adsorption efficiency of the norfloxacin antibiotic was 99.53 ± 0.13%, 99.69 ± 0.18%, 98.99 ± 0.34%, 99.04 ± 0.15%, and 99.85 ± 0.31%, respectively, for AP, PS, HZ, AP + PS, and HZ + AP + PS soot, respectively. The minimal variation in these values indicates that all soot samples exhibit a similar adsorption performance. This confirms their potential for heavy metal ion and antibiotic removal, attributed to their large surface area and the presence of active oxygenated functional groups within the soot material that act as adsorption sites for the interaction of positively charged ions. Table shows the adsorption efficiency (%) and adsorption amount (mg·g–1) of the soot material as an adsorbent in the removal of Pb­(II) and norfloxacin in an aqueous solution.

caption.title: Adsorption Efficiency and Adsorption Amount for Pb­(II) and Norfloxacin

sec.p: A comparison of carbon soot samples with other adsorbent materials for the removal of Pb­(II) is given in Table . The carbon soot samplesderived from apricot (AP), pistachio (PS), and hazelnut (HZ) shells, as well as their binary (AP + PS) and ternary (HZ + AP + PS) combinationsdemonstrate adsorption capacities of approximately 6.1 mg/g for Pb­(II) at pH 6. In terms of adsorption efficiency, the biomass-derived carbon soot sample from this work showed a high adsorption efficiency (∼91%) for Pb­(II) removal in the water sample in 60 min compared to 82.1% adsorption efficiency in 180 min from a previous work by Fatima et al. using plastic fuel-derived soot. These values are also slightly higher than those obtained from tobacco stems (5.7 mg/g), kaolin (4.50 mg/g), and fly ash (4.98 mg/g), and they considerably outperform oxidized multiwalled carbon nanotubes (2.06 mg/g) and Acacia nilotica (2.51 mg/g). This highlights the material’s promise for sustainable water treatment applications and underscores the potential benefits of converting waste biomass into high-value functional materials.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The present work reports an attempt to recycle cheap and abundant carbon soots obtained from household chimney covers after burning biomass such as the apricot shell, pistachio shell, hazelnut shell, apricot shell + pistachio shell, and hazelnut shell + apricot shell + pistachio shell. This unique concept can transform waste into a value-added material in various applications, such as an adsorbent for removing heavy metals and antibiotics, and as an electroactive material for electrochemical detections. The collected soot was characterized using XRD and Raman, which showed that the carbon soot was a highly amorphous graphite. The FTIR spectrum results showed some surface functional groups, such as oxygen-containing groups, which are potential active sites, while the morphology of the carbon soot was investigated using the SEM, showing a rough and porous network structure. The EDS analysis shows that the carbon content of the AP, PS, HZ, AP + PS, and AP + PS + HZ soot was 32.04, 38.09, 63.33, 49.51, and 75.65%, respectively, with some heteroatoms such as sulfur and potassium as the most significant that are present in all the carbon soot samples, and the HZ + AP + PS soot with the highest carbon content reflects more defects, which plays a significant role in its high electrochemical and adsorption potential. The BET results show that the HZ + AP + PS soot has the highest surface area with a mesoporous structure. Sorption experiments were performed to ascertain the impact of the physicochemical parameters of the sorption system on the adsorption of Pb­(II) and antibiotics. Higher adsorption efficiency of ∼91% and up to ∼99% was obtained at 60 min for Pb­(II) and norfloxacin antibiotic, respectively, reflecting the suitability of all the carbon soot in real wastewater treatment systems. The electrochemical performance of the carbon soot material using cyclic voltammetry (CV) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) confirmed the excellent electrochemical potential of the carbon soot materials in the following decreasing order of electrochemical performance; HZ + AP + PS > AP + PS > PS > AP > HZ, suggesting a suitable electroactive material for electrochemistry. The HZ + AP + PS soot also shows good electrochemical detection for streptomycin compared to the bare electrode. The HZ + AP + PS soot also shows good conductivity to generate electricity, with a low resistance of 3.33 Ω sq–1. Hence, the results indicate that the biomass-derived carbon soot has a great potential to be used as a sustainable and cost-effective electroactive and adsorbent material for water detoxification. Therefore, based on our findings from this work, the ternary biomass-derived carbon soot shows a promising potential, which is a new innovative way to be explored for future use in various industrial and environmental applications such as catalysis, batteries, supercapacitors, sensors, or water treatment, thereby enhancing sustainability efforts by transforming waste into functional materials. Further work suggested to be explored is the adsorption kinetics and isotherm with its regeneration capability using the ternary soots (HZ + AP + PS) and to develop an electrochemical sensor using the ternary soot (HZ + AP + PS) to quantitatively study the electrochemical detection of streptomycin from a real sample.
